tyro

TY-roh · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Tyro is a beginner or newcomer just starting out.

Though he was a tyro at woodworking, his enthusiasm for the hobby never wavered.

Example

As a tyro at chess, she still confused the names of half the pieces, but she studied every night to catch up.

Tyro is a slightly old-fashioned, literary word for a raw beginner -- someone just starting out and still learning the basics of a skill or hobby.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

newcomer: A newcomer is anyone who has just arrived -- in a town, a club, a job -- and the word is all about recent arrival, not ability: a newcomer to the city may be a master of her craft. A tyro is new to the skill itself, still finding his way through the basics.

rookie: A rookie is a first-year member of a team or force -- a label that marks the season on the calendar, not the level of skill. A tyro is defined by rawness itself: just starting out and still fumbling with the basics.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

veteran: someone highly experienced

expert: a master of the skill

Where it sits · how plainly the newness shows — learner → tyro → greenhorn

learner vs. tyro: A learner is simply someone in the middle of acquiring a skill -- the word points at the ongoing effort to learn; a tyro stands at the very start of that road, brand-new to the basics.

greenhorn vs. tyro: A greenhorn goes a step further than a tyro: not just new, but so plainly new that the inexperience shows in everything they do.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together

Put it together: Tyro comes from the Latin word tiro, meaning a young army recruit -- someone brand new to a role, with no productive root that carries into other common modern English words.

Use the root in a new word: tirocinium

Use the root in a new word: tirocinium: Latin tiro also gave us the rare word "tirocinium," meaning a period of training or apprenticeship -- a word so rare it never really caught on in English.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Tyro has a slightly formal, old-fashioned flavor -- it fits well in writing or a clever remark, but 'newbie' or 'beginner' would sound more natural in casual speech.
